title: Anansi and the Box of Stories
about: Anansi the spider climbs to the sky god Nyame to buy all the world's stories. An Akan folktale from Ghana.

scenes.text: Long ago, every story in the world belonged to Nyame, the sky god. He kept them in a golden box beside his throne, and the people below had nothing to tell around their fires at night.
Kwaku Anansi, the smallest and cleverest of spiders, spun a thread all the way up to the sky. "Great Nyame," he said, "I wish to buy your stories."

The sky court laughed. Kings had come with gold and cattle and gone home with nothing. Nyame smiled. "My price is four things: Onini the python, Osebo the leopard, Mmoboro the hornets, and Mmoatia the forest fairy."

Anansi went home and thought. For the python he cut a long palm branch and argued loudly with himself: "He is longer!" "No, shorter!" Proud Onini stretched along the branch to prove his length, and Anansi tied him fast.

For the leopard he dug a deep pit across Osebo's path and covered it with leaves. In the morning the great cat lay at the bottom, growling, and Anansi "helped" him out with a rope that held him tight.
For the hornets he filled a calabash with water, poured some over their nest and shouted, "It is raining! Hide in my gourd!" The hornets flew in, and Anansi plugged the hole with grass.
For Mmoatia he carved a little doll, covered it in sticky gum and set a bowl of mashed yam before it. The fairy ate, said thank you, and when the doll did not answer she slapped it, and stuck fast.
Anansi climbed back up his thread with the python, the leopard, the hornets and the fairy. The sky court fell silent. Nyame rose from his throne.
"Kings could not pay my price, but Anansi has," said Nyame. "From today, the stories belong to him." He opened the golden box, and the stories tumbled down to every village.

That is why, among the Akan, stories are called Anansesem: spider stories. And whenever a griot finishes a tale, he says: this is my story, which I have told; if it be sweet, take some elsewhere, and let some come back to me.

title: Anansi and the Python
about: Clever Anansi tricks the proud python Onini with a palm branch. A tale of wit over strength from Ghana.

scenes.text: Onini the python was the longest creature in the forest, and he never let anyone forget it. He coiled in the sun by the river and laughed at the small ones as they passed.
Anansi needed Onini for the sky god's price, but no spider can carry a python. So he sat under the python's tree and began to argue with himself, loud enough for the whole forest to hear.
"He is longer than this palm branch!" said Anansi. Then, in a different voice: "No, he is shorter! The branch is longer!" Onini lifted his great head. "Who is shorter than a branch?"
"My wife says you are shorter than this palm branch," said Anansi sadly. "I said you were longer. Now we will never know." "Bring it here," hissed Onini. "I will show you."
The python stretched himself along the branch as straight as a spear. "Your tail slips back when you stretch your head," said Anansi. "Let me tie it, so the measure is fair."
He tied the tail. Then the middle. Then, just to be sure, the neck. When Onini understood the trick, it was too late: he was bound to the branch from head to tail.
Anansi carried the branch to the sky god. And the elders say: strength boasts in the sun, but wisdom works quietly in the shade.

title: Mami Wata and the Fisher Girl
about: A brave fisher girl follows a glowing python into the water queen's palace. A legend of West Africa's water spirit.

scenes.text: In a fishing village by the lagoon lived a girl named Adjoa. Every dawn she paddled out with her grandmother's net, and every evening she shared her catch with the old people who could no longer fish.
One season the fish vanished. The nets came up empty, the children grew thin, and the elders said the lagoon was angry with the village.
That night Adjoa saw a light under the water: a python glowing like a lantern, swimming in slow circles beside her canoe. It looked at her, then dived.

Adjoa took a breath and followed. Down she went, past the reeds, past the sleeping crabs, to a palace of shells where a woman sat with a great python wrapped around her shoulders. It was Mami Wata, queen of the waters.
"Your people throw rubbish into my lagoon and take my youngest fish before they can grow," said the queen. "Why should I send them back?"
"Because I will teach my people to take only the grown fish and keep the water clean," said Adjoa. "And because the old ones are hungry." The queen saw that the girl spoke the truth.
Adjoa woke in her canoe at sunrise, her net heavy with silver fish. She kept her promise: the village made new rules for the lagoon, and the fish returned year after year.
To this day, along the coast from Ghana to Nigeria and beyond, people speak of Mami Wata: beautiful, powerful, and generous to those who respect the water.

title: Zuba and the Griot
about: Zuba sits by the fire as an old griot tells how stories keep a people alive.

scenes.text: The night was cool and the stars were thick over the village. Zuba the puppy curled up by the fire, his kente scarf pulled close.
An old griot sat down with his kora, a harp with twenty-one strings. He plucked one note, and the whole circle went quiet.
"Do you know why I sing, little one?" asked the griot. Zuba shook his ears. "Because a people without stories is like a tree without roots. The first wind will knock it down."
He sang of kings who built cities of mud and gold, of grandmothers who saved their villages with clever words, of hunters who learned to listen to the forest.
"Every name I sing," said the griot, "is a lamp. As long as someone remembers it, it does not go out."
Zuba looked at the faces around the fire: children, parents, elders, all listening together. He understood that the stories belonged to all of them.
When the fire burned low, the griot put down his kora. "Now it is your turn," he said to Zuba. "Learn the words of your people, and carry the light."

title: Sundiata: Lion King of Mali
about: The boy who could not walk rises, wins the battle of Kirina and founds the Mali Empire, as the griots tell it.

scenes.text: Eight hundred years ago, in the land of Manden on the upper Niger, a soothsayer told King Naré Maghan Konaté that he must marry a plain woman, and that her son would become a great king.
The woman was Sogolon, and her son was Sundiata. But the boy could not walk. Year after year he crawled, and the other wives of the palace laughed at Sogolon and her son.

One day Sogolon wept because she had no baobab leaves to cook, and the queen mother mocked her. Sundiata called for an iron rod. Leaning on it, he pulled himself up. The rod bent like a bow, but Sundiata stood.
The griots sing that he walked to the baobab tree, pulled it out of the ground and laid it at his mother's door. From that day, no one laughed at Sogolon again.

When the old king died, the jealous queen mother threatened Sundiata's life. Sogolon fled with her children, travelling for years from kingdom to kingdom. Sundiata grew strong and learned the ways of kings and armies.
Meanwhile Soumaoro Kanté, the sorcerer king of Sosso, conquered Manden. He was cruel and feared, and his magic was said to make him impossible to defeat.
The people of Manden sent messengers to find Sundiata. He gathered allies from many kingdoms and marched home. His griot, Balla Fasséké, sang to give the warriors courage.
His sister Nana Triban had learned Soumaoro's secret: his power would fail if he was touched by the spur of a white rooster. Sundiata tied the spur to the tip of an arrow.
At the battle of Kirina, around the year 1235, the arrow grazed Soumaoro's shoulder. The sorcerer king felt his magic leave him. He fled into the mountains, and was never seen again.
Sundiata gathered the leaders of the land at Kurukan Fuga and agreed the laws that would bind the clans together. The Mali Empire was born, with Sundiata as its first Mansa, its king of kings.
Mali grew rich on gold and trade, and a century later his descendant Mansa Musa amazed the world. But it all began with a boy who could not walk, and a mother who never stopped believing.
Griots of the Kouyaté family, descendants of Balla Fasséké, still sing this story today, passing it from parent to child, as they have for eight hundred years.

title: Thomas Sankara: The Upright Man
about: The young president who renamed his country Burkina Faso, planted millions of trees and spoke for dignity and self-reliance.

scenes.text: Thomas Sankara was born in 1949 in Yako, in the French colony then called Upper Volta. He grew up as a curious, hard-working boy who loved music and asked a great many questions.
He became a soldier and a guitarist, known for his honesty and his laugh. On 4 August 1983, at just 33 years old, he became the country's leader.
In 1984 he gave his country a new name: Burkina Faso, made from words in the Mooré and Dioula languages. It means the land of upright, honest people.
He sold the government's fleet of expensive cars and asked his ministers to drive small, simple ones. Leaders, he said, should live like the people they serve.
In 1984 a nationwide campaign vaccinated around two and a half million children against measles, meningitis and yellow fever in about two weeks.
Families planted more than ten million trees to hold back the Sahara desert. Villages built schools and clinics with their own hands.
He spoke out for women's rights. Women became ministers and soldiers, and he worked to end forced marriage and other harmful practices.
"He who feeds you, controls you," he said, urging Burkinabè to grow and buy their own food and wear cotton woven at home.
On 15 October 1987, Thomas Sankara was killed in a coup. He was 37. In 2022, a court in Ouagadougou found those responsible guilty.
His words still travel across Africa and the world. Many young people remember him as the upright man who believed his country could stand on its own feet.

title: Patrice Lumumba: Voice of Congo
about: From a post office desk to the independence stage in 1960: the story of Congo's first prime minister.

scenes.text: Patrice Émery Lumumba was born in 1925 in Onalua, in the Kasai region of the Belgian Congo. He loved to read, and taught himself much of what he knew.
As a young man he worked as a postal clerk in Stanleyville, today's Kisangani. He wrote essays and poems, and began to speak about the right of the Congolese people to govern themselves.
In 1958 he became a leader of the Mouvement National Congolais, one of the first movements to call for a united, independent Congo for all its peoples, not just one region or group.
He was arrested for his speeches, but the call for freedom grew too strong. Belgium agreed to hold elections, and Lumumba's party won the most seats.
On 30 June 1960 the Congo became independent. Before the King of Belgium and the world, Lumumba gave a speech about the suffering of colonial rule and the dignity of his people.
He became the Congo's first prime minister, at 34 years old. But the young country faced enormous troubles: a mutiny in the army, and the rich province of Katanga trying to break away.
Within months, Lumumba was removed from power and arrested. On 17 January 1961 he was killed in Katanga. He was 35 years old.
In 2002 the Belgian government apologised for its part in the events that led to his death. In 2022, a tooth, the only remains of Lumumba ever found, was returned to his family in Kinshasa.
In a letter to his wife he wrote that history would one day have its say, and that it would be Africa's own history.
Today Lumumba is remembered across Africa as a symbol of courage, unity and the dream of true independence.

title: Zuba: Kingdom in the Sky
about: Zuba glides on threads of kente light between floating islands, rainforest giants and ancient stone masks.

scenes.text: One morning Zuba found a thread of light hanging from the clouds, woven in the gold and green of kente cloth. He gave it a tug, and it pulled him into the sky.
Above the clouds floated islands covered in rainforest, linked by more glowing threads. Waterfalls poured off their edges and turned to mist before they reached the ground.
On the first island the trees were so tall that their roots hung in the air like curtains. Grey parrots taught Zuba to say hello in Twi: "Maakye!"
The threads led to an island of stone masks, each as big as a house. Their eyes followed Zuba as he passed, and the oldest mask spoke: "Only one who knows our words may cross."
Zuba remembered the words he had learned on his journey: hello, thank you, friend. With each word, a new thread of light appeared across the gap.
At the highest island stood a palace of clouds, where the kingdom's guardians kept the colours of every cloth ever woven in Africa.
"You crossed the sky with words, not wings," said the guardian. "Take this thread home, and weave your own story." Zuba slid back to earth on a ribbon of sunset.

title: Zuba: Sahel Night Run
about: Zuba dashes across a moonlit mud-brick city, chased by shadow spirits.

scenes.text: Under a full moon, the mud-brick city of the Sahel glowed silver. The towers of its great mosque bristled with wooden beams, like a giant porcupine asleep in the sand.
Zuba was carrying a scroll to the city's library when the shadows began to move. Shadow spirits, who feed on forgotten words, had smelled the scroll.
Zuba ran. He leapt from roof to roof, slid under drying racks of indigo cloth and bounced off the wooden beams that the builders use to repair the walls after the rains.
Each time a shadow came close, Zuba shouted a word from the scroll, and the light of it pushed the spirit back into the dark.
At last he reached the library door. The old librarian opened it, and the shadows hissed and melted away in the lamplight.
"Scholars have kept these manuscripts safe for hundreds of years," said the librarian. "Every word you carry is a light in the dark." Zuba wagged his tail and went home under the stars.

title: Oware Kings
about: Two kings settle a war over a board of seeds. A tale of oware, the great strategy game of the Akan.

scenes.text: Oware is one of the oldest games in Africa. Two players face each other across a board of twelve small pits, sowing forty-eight seeds around and around, trying to capture more than their rival.
The Ashanti tell of two kings whose kingdoms were ready for war. Their armies stood on either side of a river, spears in hand, waiting for the order.
But the queen mothers of both kingdoms crossed the river together. "Why waste your young men's lives?" they asked. "Let the kings settle this with a game of oware."
The kings sat down at a board carved from a single log. The armies gathered around to watch. Each king scooped up the seeds from one pit and sowed them, one by one, into the pits that followed.
The game went on all day and into the night. Each king planned many moves ahead, saving seeds in his largest pit, waiting for the moment to capture.
In oware you must never leave your opponent with no seeds to play, the elders say, for even in a contest, you must let your rival live.
At dawn the game was so close that neither king could win. They laughed, embraced and married their children to each other, joining the two kingdoms in peace.
People still play oware in Ghana, across West Africa and the Caribbean. And when two friends argue, the old ones sometimes say: go and play oware, and come back as brothers.

title: Impundulu: Sky Racer
about: A young rider races the lightning bird of southern African legend through the storms above the Drakensberg.

scenes.text: In the stories of the Zulu, Xhosa and Mpondo peoples, the Impundulu is a lightning bird as tall as a man, with black and white feathers. When it beats its wings, thunder rolls; when it dives, lightning strikes.
A young herder named Sipho watched the summer storms gather over the Drakensberg mountains every afternoon. He dreamed of flying with them.
One evening a storm swept the cattle into a panic. As lightning split the sky, Sipho saw it: the Impundulu itself, circling above the herd.
"Leave my cattle alone!" shouted Sipho. The lightning bird laughed like rolling thunder. "Catch me, little herder, and I will."
Sipho grabbed a feather as the bird swept low, and was lifted into the storm. They raced through rings of cloud painted in bright Ndebele patterns, over peaks and waterfalls.
Sipho held on with all his strength. He did not let go when the bird dived, or when it climbed so high the air turned to ice.
At last the Impundulu landed on the highest peak. "No one has held on so long," it said. "Your cattle are safe tonight." It flew off, and the storm went with it.
Since then, the old people say, when lightning flashes but does not strike the herd, it is the Impundulu remembering a brave young herder.

title: Grootslang Caves
about: Explore deep caves with San rock art and face the Grootslang, the great serpent of South African legend.

scenes.text: In the dry hills of the Richtersveld in South Africa, people speak of the Grootslang: a giant creature with the body of a serpent and the head of an elephant, older than the mountains.
Its name means great snake in Afrikaans. The legend says it lives in a bottomless cave called the Wonder Hole, guarding a hoard of diamonds.
A young explorer named Lerato followed an old map into the hills. At the cave mouth she found paintings made by San artists long ago: eland, dancers and a great snake with tusks.
Inside, her lamp lit up walls of glittering crystal. Water dripped somewhere far below, and a cold breath came up from the dark.
Then the floor moved. Two great tusks rose from the shadows, and the Grootslang lifted its head. "Many have come for my diamonds," it rumbled. "None have returned."
Lerato set down her pack. "I did not come for diamonds," she said. "I came to see the paintings, and to learn the story."
The Grootslang was silent for a long time. Then it lowered its head. "Then you may go," it said, "and tell them the cave is not for the greedy."
Lerato climbed out into the sunlight with nothing in her pockets but her notebook, full of drawings. It was the greatest treasure she ever found.

title: Ninki Nanka
about: A hunter in the Gambian swamps faces the legendary river dragon of West Africa.

scenes.text: In the mangrove swamps along the Gambia River, people tell of the Ninki Nanka, a dragon longer than a canoe, with a crest on its head and scales that shine like mirrors.
The legend warns that anyone who looks straight at the Ninki Nanka will fall sick. Children are told never to wander alone into the deep swamp.
A hunter named Lamin did not believe the old stories. He paddled into the swamp at dusk to hunt, laughing at his grandmother's warnings.
As the light faded, the water began to ripple in great slow circles. Birds fell silent. Lamin felt eyes watching him from the reeds.
He remembered his grandmother's words: if you ever feel the dragon near, close your eyes, speak with respect, and leave its home in peace.
Lamin tied a cloth over his eyes. "I am sorry I came uninvited," he said. "I will go now." He paddled back slowly, by feel and by sound.
When he pulled the cloth away, he was at the edge of his village, and the water behind him was still.
From then on Lamin was the first to warn young hunters about the deep swamp. For some stories, he said, are not told to frighten us, but to keep us alive.
